rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He identifies the sūra as Meccan and says it has five verses.
rows.anchor: مقدمة السورة: مكية ، وآياتها خمس .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabāb means destruction; the expression أشابة أم تابة describes someone ruined by old age and debility.
rows.anchor: التباب : الهلاك . ومنه قولهم : أشابة أم تابة ؟ أي : هالكة من الهرم والتعجيز .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He initially interprets the phrase as a curse that Abu Lahab's hands perished.
rows.anchor: هلكت يداه ؛ لأنه فيما يروى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes wa-tabba as saying that Abu Lahab himself perished entirely.
rows.anchor: { وَتَبَّ } وهلك كله .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Abu Lahab picked up a stone to throw at the Messenger, explaining the curse that his hands perish.
rows.anchor: لأنه فيما يروى : أخذ حجراً ليرمي به رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, his hands are made to perish, with the hands standing for his whole person; Zamakhsharī compares 22:10.
rows.anchor: أو جعلت يداه هالكتين . والمراد : هلاك جملته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, wa-tabba means that the matter happened and came to pass; he supports this completed-event sense with a poetic line ending وقد فعل.
rows.anchor: جَزَانِي جَزَاهُ اللَّهُ شَرَّ جَزَائِه *** جَزَاءَ الْكلاَبِ الْعَاوِيَاتِ وَقَدْ فَعَلْ

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads وقد تب, which Zamakhsharī cites to support the sense that the matter had indeed come to pass.
rows.anchor: ويدلّ عليه قراءة ابن مسعود : «وقد تب »

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says that after 26:214 was revealed, the Prophet called his clan at Ṣafā, tested whether they would believe a warning about cavalry at the mountain, then warned them of the Hour; Abu Lahab protested, and this sūra was revealed.
rows.anchor: وروي : أنه لما نزل { وَأَنذِرْ عَشِيرَتَكَ الأقربين } [ الشعراء : 214 ]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His first answer to why an ostensibly honorific kunya is used is that Abu Lahab was better known by it, making the hostile designation conspicuous and lasting.
rows.anchor: أن يكون مشتهراً بالكنية دون الاسم ، فقد يكون الرجل معروفاً بأحدهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person may be known by either name or kunya, and the two can stand in apposition in either order.
rows.anchor: ولذلك تجري الكنية على الاسم ، أو الاسم على الكنية عطف بيان

rows.speaker: غير مسمى
rows.claim: An unnamed reader has يدا أبو لهب, preserving the familiar form Abū Lahab and supporting the first explanation for using his kunya.
rows.anchor: ويؤيد ذلك قراءة من قرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites forms such as ʿAlī ibn Abū Ṭālib and Muʿāwiya ibn Abū Sufyān, where Abū is left unchanged so altering the familiar form will not confuse the hearer.
rows.anchor: كما قيل : علي بن أبو طالب . ومعاوية بن أبو سفيان ؛ لئلا يغير منه شيء فيشكل على السامع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He illustrates the importance of familiar name forms with Meccan governor Fulayta ibn Qasim's two sons, both called ʿAbd Allāh, one marked genitive and the other accusative; a Meccan man was known only by the genitive form.
rows.anchor: ولفليتة بن قاسم أمير مكة ابنان ، أحدهما : عبد الله ، بالجرّ ، والآخر عبد الله ، بالنصب .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation is that Abu Lahab's personal name was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, so the kunya was used in its place.
rows.anchor: والثاني : أنه كان اسمه عبد العزّى ، فعدل عنه إلى كنيته .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation is that his fate in a fire with flames matches his kunya, making it fitting to name him by it.
rows.anchor: والثالث : أنه لما كان من أهل النار ، ومآله إلى نار ذات لهب ، وافقت حاله كنيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Lahab can function as a trait-based label, like Abū al-Sharr for an evil person and Abū al-Khayr for a good one.
rows.anchor: ويقال : أبو لهب ، كما يقال : أبو الشر ، للشرير . وأبو الخير ، للخير

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: As an example of a trait-based kunya, the Messenger called Abū al-Muhallab Abū Ṣafra because of the yellow color in his face.
rows.anchor: كما كنى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أبا المهلب : أبا صفرة ، بصفرة في وجهه .

rows.speaker: غير مسمى
rows.claim: An alternative account says he was called Abū Lahab for his flushed, radiant cheeks.
rows.anchor: وقيل : كنى بذلك لتهلب وجنتيه وإشراقهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zamakhsharī suggests that using the kunya this way could mock Abu Lahab and his pride in his bright cheeks.
rows.anchor: فيجوز أن يذكر بذلك تهكماً به ، وبافتخاره بذلك .

rows.speaker: غير مسمى
rows.claim: A reading gives أبي لهب with sukūn; Zamakhsharī treats it as an alteration of proper names, like saying Shams ibn Mālik with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وهو من تغيير الأعلام ، كقولهم
